claim: Perceptual confidence is an evaluation of the validity of perceptual decisions.
source: Perceptual confidence is an evaluation of the validity of perceptual decisions.
evidence: This is a definitional statement presented in the abstract that establishes the concept being studied.

claim: There is behavioural evidence that confidence evaluation differs from perceptual decision-making.
source: While there is behavioural evidence that confidence evaluation differs from perceptual decision-making, disentangling these two processes remains a challenge at the neural level.
evidence: The statement references existing behavioral evidence without specific citations in this sentence, drawing on established findings in the field.

claim: Observers tend to commit to perceptual decisions early whilst continuing to monitor sensory evidence for evaluating confidence in protracted perceptual decision-making tasks.
source: Here, we examined the electrical brain activity of human participants in a protracted perceptual decision-making task where observers tend to commit to perceptual decisions early whilst continuing to monitor sensory evidence for evaluating confidence.
evidence: This is a primary finding from the current study as stated in the abstract.

claim: Premature decision commitments are revealed by patterns of spectral power overlying motor cortex.
source: Premature decision commitments were revealed by patterns of spectral power overlying motor cortex, followed by an attenuation of the neural representation of perceptual decision evidence.
evidence: This is a direct finding from the EEG analysis presented in the study.

claim: Premature decision commitments are followed by an attenuation of the neural representation of perceptual decision evidence.
source: Premature decision commitments were revealed by patterns of spectral power overlying motor cortex, followed by an attenuation of the neural representation of perceptual decision evidence.
evidence: This is a direct finding from the neural representation analysis in the study.

claim: A distinct neural representation is associated with the computation of confidence, with sources localised in the superior parietal and orbitofrontal cortices.
source: A distinct neural representation was associated with the computation of confidence, with sources localised in the superior parietal and orbitofrontal cortices.
evidence: This is a primary finding from the source localization analysis presented in the study.

claim: Neural resources for confidence evaluation are recruited even after observers committed to their perceptual decisions.
source: In agreement with a dissociation between perception and confidence, these neural resources were recruited even after observers committed to their perceptual decisions, and thus delineate an integral neural circuit for evaluating perceptual decision confidence.
evidence: This is a finding from the temporal analysis of neural representations in the study.

claim: Perception requires probabilistic inference to resolve the uncertain causes of essentially ambiguous sensory input.
source: Whilst perception typically feels effortless and automatic, it requires probabilistic inference to resolve the uncertain causes of essentially ambiguous sensory input (Helmholtz, 1856).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Helmholtz (1856), representing established theory in perception.

claim: Human observers are capable of discriminating which perceptual decisions are more likely to be correct using subjective feelings of confidence.
source: Human observers are capable of discriminating which perceptual decisions are more likely to be correct using subjective feelings of confidence (Pollack and Decker, 1958).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Pollack and Decker (1958), representing established empirical findings.

claim: Feelings of perceptual confidence have been associated with metacognitive processes.
source: These feelings of perceptual confidence have been associated with metacognitive processes (Fleming and Daw, 2017) that enable self-monitoring for learning (Veenman et al., 2004) and communication (Bahrami et al., 2012; Frith, 2012).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to Fleming and Daw (2017), Veenman et al. (2004), Bahrami et al. (2012), and Frith (2012).

claim: Metacognitive processes enable self-monitoring for learning.
source: These feelings of perceptual confidence have been associated with metacognitive processes (Fleming and Daw, 2017) that enable self-monitoring for learning (Veenman et al., 2004) and communication (Bahrami et al., 2012; Frith, 2012).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Veenman et al. (2004).

claim: Metacognitive processes enable communication.
source: These feelings of perceptual confidence have been associated with metacognitive processes (Fleming and Daw, 2017) that enable self-monitoring for learning (Veenman et al., 2004) and communication (Bahrami et al., 2012; Frith, 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Bahrami et al. (2012) and Frith (2012).

claim: Perceptual decisions are described by sequential sampling processes at the computational level.
source: At the computational level, perceptual decisions are described by sequential sampling processes (Ratcliff, 1978; Vickers, 1970), in which noisy samples of evidence are accumulated over time, until there is sufficient evidence to commit to a decision.
evidence: This is supported by citations to Ratcliff (1978) and Vickers (1970), representing established computational models.

claim: In sequential sampling processes, noisy samples of evidence are accumulated over time until there is sufficient evidence to commit to a decision.
source: At the computational level, perceptual decisions are described by sequential sampling processes (Ratcliff, 1978; Vickers, 1970), in which noisy samples of evidence are accumulated over time, until there is sufficient evidence to commit to a decision.
evidence: This is a description of the sequential sampling framework supported by the cited references.

claim: The most relevant information for evaluating perceptual confidence is the quantity and quality of evidence used to make the perceptual decision.
source: The most relevant information for evaluating perceptual confidence is the quantity and quality of evidence used to make the perceptual decision (Kepecs et al., 2008; Moreno-Bote, 2010; Vickers, 1979).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Kepecs et al. (2008), Moreno-Bote (2010), and Vickers (1979).

claim: Confidence can be reliably predicted from the firing rates of neurons coding the perceptual decision itself.
source: Indeed, confidence (or a non-human primate proxy for confidence) can be reliably predicted from the firing rates of neurons coding the perceptual decision itself (Kiani and Shadlen, 2009), suggesting that confidence may be a direct by-product of perceptual processing.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Kiani and Shadlen (2009), representing empirical findings from neurophysiology.

claim: Confidence may be a direct by-product of perceptual processing.
source: Indeed, confidence (or a non-human primate proxy for confidence) can be reliably predicted from the firing rates of neurons coding the perceptual decision itself (Kiani and Shadlen, 2009), suggesting that confidence may be a direct by-product of perceptual processing.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the cited neurophysiological findings.

claim: Confidence can integrate additional evidence after the observer commits to their perceptual decision.
source: Confidence can integrate additional evidence after the observer commits to their perceptual decision (Pleskac and Busemeyer, 2010; Baranski and Petrusic, 1994), and while this continued evidence accumulation could incorporate only perceptual information, it implies that confidence evaluation does not directly follow from perceptual decision commitment (and therefore involves at least partially dissociable neural processes).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Pleskac and Busemeyer (2010) and Baranski and Petrusic (1994).

claim: Confidence evaluation does not directly follow from perceptual decision commitment.
source: Confidence can integrate additional evidence after the observer commits to their perceptual decision (Pleskac and Busemeyer, 2010; Baranski and Petrusic, 1994), and while this continued evidence accumulation could incorporate only perceptual information, it implies that confidence evaluation does not directly follow from perceptual decision commitment (and therefore involves at least partially dissociable neural processes).
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the cited behavioral findings about post-decisional evidence integration.

claim: Confidence evaluation involves at least partially dissociable neural processes from perceptual decision-making.
source: Confidence can integrate additional evidence after the observer commits to their perceptual decision (Pleskac and Busemeyer, 2010; Baranski and Petrusic, 1994), and while this continued evidence accumulation could incorporate only perceptual information, it implies that confidence evaluation does not directly follow from perceptual decision commitment (and therefore involves at least partially dissociable neural processes).
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the behavioral evidence of post-decisional integration.

claim: Perceptual confidence can rely on separate non-perceptual sources of information such as decision time.
source: There is also evidence that perceptual confidence can rely on separate (non-perceptual) sources of information, such as decision time (Kiani et al., 2014) and attentional cues (Denison et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Kiani et al. (2014).

claim: Perceptual confidence can rely on separate non-perceptual sources of information such as attentional cues.
source: There is also evidence that perceptual confidence can rely on separate (non-perceptual) sources of information, such as decision time (Kiani et al., 2014) and attentional cues (Denison et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Denison et al. (2018).

claim: Confidence precision is correlated across different cognitive tasks such as memory and perception.
source: Indeed, there is some evidence that confidence precision is correlated across different cognitive tasks (such as memory and perception; Mazancieux et al., 2020), suggesting a common source of noise affecting the computation of confidence across tasks (on top of the sensory noise; Bang et al., 2019; Shekhar and Rahnev, 2021).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Mazancieux et al. (2020).

claim: There is a common source of noise affecting the computation of confidence across tasks on top of sensory noise.
source: Indeed, there is some evidence that confidence precision is correlated across different cognitive tasks (such as memory and perception; Mazancieux et al., 2020), suggesting a common source of noise affecting the computation of confidence across tasks (on top of the sensory noise; Bang et al., 2019; Shekhar and Rahnev, 2021).
evidence: This is an inference supported by citations to Bang et al. (2019) and Shekhar and Rahnev (2021).

claim: Modulations in confidence have been linked with activity in subregions of the prefrontal cortex including the orbitofrontal cortex.
source: Several experiments have linked modulations in confidence with activity in a variety of subregions of the prefrontal cortex (including the orbitofrontal cortex, Lak et al., 2014; Masset et al., 2020; right frontopolar cortex, Yokoyama et al., 2010; rostro-lateral prefrontal cortex, Fleming et al., 2012; Geurts et al., 2021; Cortese et al., 2016; see also Vaccaro and Fleming, 2018, for a meta-analysis).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Lak et al. (2014) and Masset et al. (2020).

claim: Modulations in confidence have been linked with activity in the right frontopolar cortex.
source: Several experiments have linked modulations in confidence with activity in a variety of subregions of the prefrontal cortex (including the orbitofrontal cortex, Lak et al., 2014; Masset et al., 2020; right frontopolar cortex, Yokoyama et al., 2010; rostro-lateral prefrontal cortex, Fleming et al., 2012; Geurts et al., 2021; Cortese et al., 2016; see also Vaccaro and Fleming, 2018, for a meta-analysis).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Yokoyama et al. (2010).

claim: Modulations in confidence have been linked with activity in the rostro-lateral prefrontal cortex.
source: Several experiments have linked modulations in confidence with activity in a variety of subregions of the prefrontal cortex (including the orbitofrontal cortex, Lak et al., 2014; Masset et al., 2020; right frontopolar cortex, Yokoyama et al., 2010; rostro-lateral prefrontal cortex, Fleming et al., 2012; Geurts et al., 2021; Cortese et al., 2016; see also Vaccaro and Fleming, 2018, for a meta-analysis).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Fleming et al. (2012), Geurts et al. (2021), and Cortese et al. (2016).

claim: Disrupting processing in subregions of the prefrontal cortex tends to impair the ability to appropriately adjust behavioural confidence responses whilst leaving perceptual decision accuracy largely unaffected.
source: Moreover, disrupting the processing in subregions of the prefrontal cortex (Fleming et al., 2014; Lak et al., 2014; Rounis et al., 2010) tends to impair (though not obliterate) the ability to appropriately adjust behavioural confidence responses, whilst leaving perceptual decision accuracy largely unaffected (although these results can be difficult to replicate, Bor et al., 2017; Lapate et al., 2020, and may not generalise to metacognition for memory; Fleming et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Fleming et al. (2014), Lak et al. (2014), and Rounis et al. (2010), with caveats noted from Bor et al. (2017) and Lapate et al. (2020).

claim: Post-decisional changes in confidence magnitude correlate with signals from the posterior medial frontal cortex.
source: These studies show that post-decisional changes in confidence magnitude correlate with signals from the posterior medial frontal cortex.
evidence: This refers to findings from studies mentioned in the preceding sentence (Fleming et al., 2018; Murphy et al., 2015).

claim: Error signals drive medial frontal activity more strongly than decision accuracy.
source: However, these signals could reflect processes occurring downstream of confidence, such as an emotional response to the error signal, which has been shown to drive medial frontal activity more strongly than decision accuracy (Gehring and Willoughby, 2002).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Gehring and Willoughby (2002).

claim: Perceptual decision sensitivity (d') was significantly decreased with two fewer stimuli in the Less condition compared to the Free task.
source: Replicating these previous results (Balsdon et al., 2020), we found that perceptual decision sensitivity (d') was significantly decreased with just two fewer stimuli in the Less condition compared to those same (pmin) trials in the Free task (Wilcoxon sign rank Z = 3.88, p < 0.001, Bonferroni corrected for three comparisons), but four additional stimuli in the More condition resulted in only a small but not significant increase compared to the pmax trials in the Free task (Z = -1.53, p = 0.13, uncorrected).
evidence: This is a statistical finding from the behavioral analysis of the current study.

claim: Four additional stimuli in the More condition resulted in only a small but not significant increase in perceptual decision sensitivity compared to the Free task.
source: Replicating these previous results (Balsdon et al., 2020), we found that perceptual decision sensitivity (d') was significantly decreased with just two fewer stimuli in the Less condition compared to those same (pmin) trials in the Free task (Wilcoxon sign rank Z = 3.88, p < 0.001, Bonferroni corrected for three comparisons), but four additional stimuli in the More condition resulted in only a small but not significant increase compared to the pmax trials in the Free task (Z = -1.53, p = 0.13, uncorrected).
evidence: This is a statistical finding from the behavioral analysis of the current study.

claim: Cross-validated model comparison provided significant evidence that observers were implementing a covert bound.
source: Cross-validated model comparison provided significant evidence that observers were implementing a covert bound (mean relative increase in model log-likelihood = 0.048, bootstrapped p = 0.001, Figure 2c).
evidence: This is a finding from the computational modeling analysis, with reference to Figure 2c.

claim: There was no evidence that observers were implementing a covert bound on confidence.
source: In contrast to what we found for the perceptual decision, there was no evidence that observers were implementing a covert bound on confidence: Implementing the same bound as the perceptual decision did not improve the fit (relative improvement with bound = −0.007, bootstrapped p = 0.11, uncorrected) and an independent bound actually significantly reduced the fit compared to continued accumulation (relative improvement = −0.014, p = 0.022, Bonferroni corrected for two comparisons; Figure 2c).
evidence: This is a finding from the computational modeling analysis, with reference to Figure 2c.

claim: The best description of both perceptual and confidence responses was provided by a partially dissociated computational architecture where perceptual and confidence decisions are based on the same noisy representation of the sensory evidence, but confidence accumulation incurs additional noise and can continue after the completion of perceptual decision processes.
source: The best description of both perceptual and confidence responses was provided by a partially dissociated computational architecture (full details in Appendix 1), where perceptual and confidence decisions are based on the same noisy representation of the sensory evidence, but confidence accumulation incurs additional noise and can continue after the completion of perceptual decision processes (Figure 2d, and the predictions of this model for individual participants are show in Figure 2e).
evidence: This is a finding from the computational modeling analysis, with references to Figures 2d and 2e.

claim: The presented evidence accumulated over all samples explains substantial variance in observers' perceptual decisions.
source: First, we find the presented evidence accumulated over all samples does explain substantial variance in observers' perceptual decisions (average β = 0.77, t(19) = 6.48, p < 0.001), and confidence evaluations (with the evidence signed by the perceptual response; β = 0.24, t(19) = 6.46, p < 0.001).
evidence: This is a statistical finding from the GLM analysis of the current study.

claim: The presented evidence accumulated over all samples explains substantial variance in observers' confidence evaluations.
source: First, we find the presented evidence accumulated over all samples does explain substantial variance in observers' perceptual decisions (average β = 0.77, t(19) = 6.48, p < 0.001), and confidence evaluations (with the evidence signed by the perceptual response; β = 0.24, t(19) = 6.46, p < 0.001).
evidence: This is a statistical finding from the GLM analysis of the current study.

claim: The total accumulated evidence in the More condition was not a significantly better predictor of observers' perceptual decisions than the evidence up to four samples prior to the response.
source: Second, the total accumulated evidence in the More condition was not a significantly better predictor of the observers' perceptual decisions than the evidence up to four samples prior to the response (average difference in β = 0.034, t(19) = 1.63, p = 0.12), while for the Same and Less conditions the total accumulated evidence was a significantly better predictor (Less: t(19) = 4.99, p < 0.001; Same: t(19) = 3.11, p = 0.006; causing a significant interaction between condition and sample accumulated to F(2,38) = 10.348, p = 0.001, Bonferroni corrected for three comparisons, Figure 2f, top).
evidence: This is a statistical finding from the GLM analysis, with reference to Figure 2f.

claim: For the Same and Less conditions, the total accumulated evidence was a significantly better predictor of perceptual decisions than evidence accumulated to four samples prior.
source: Second, the total accumulated evidence in the More condition was not a significantly better predictor of the observers' perceptual decisions than the evidence up to four samples prior to the response (average difference in β = 0.034, t(19) = 1.63, p = 0.12), while for the Same and Less conditions the total accumulated evidence was a significantly better predictor (Less: t(19) = 4.99, p < 0.001; Same: t(19) = 3.11, p = 0.006; causing a significant interaction between condition and sample accumulated to F(2,38) = 10.348, p = 0.001, Bonferroni corrected for three comparisons, Figure 2f, top).
evidence: This is a statistical finding from the GLM analysis, with reference to Figure 2f.

claim: The accumulated evidence up to the final sample in the More condition was a significantly better predictor of confidence than the evidence accumulated to four samples from the response.
source: Rather, the accumulated evidence up to the final sample in the More condition was a significantly better predictor of confidence than the evidence accumulated to four samples from the response (average difference in β = 0.26, t(19) = 5.33, p < 0.001), supporting the prediction from the computational model analysis that observers integrated all the presented evidence for evaluating confidence.
evidence: This is a statistical finding from the GLM analysis of the current study.

claim: Spectral power in the 8 to 32 Hz frequency range could be used to classify perceptual decisions based on lateralised differences over motor cortex.
source: Initial analysis suggested the spectral power in the 8 to 32 Hz frequency range (the 'alpha' and 'beta' bands) could be used to classify perceptual decisions based on lateralised differences over motor cortex (Appendix 5).
evidence: This is a finding from the EEG spectral analysis of the current study.

claim: Training around −0.78 to 0.44 s from the time of the response in the Free task led to significantly better accuracy testing in the More condition than in the Less condition, prior to when the response was entered.
source: Statistical comparison revealed substantial clusters of significant differences (Figure 3b): Training around −0.78 to 0.44 s from the time of the response in the Free task led to significantly better accuracy testing in the More condition than in the Less condition, prior to when the response was entered (for the cluster testing at −2.5 to −1.6 s Zave = 2.04, pcluster = 0.002; testing at −1.5 to −1 s, Zave = 1.95, pcluster = 0.01; testing at −0.8 to −0.3, Zave = 2.32, pcluster < 0.001).
evidence: This is a statistical finding from the cross-classification analysis, with reference to Figure 3b.

claim: Observers were not only committing to their perceptual decision early, but already preparing their motor response.
source: This pattern of findings suggests that observers were not only committing to their perceptual decision early, but already preparing their motor response.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the cross-classification analysis results.

claim: The optimal evidence L accumulated over all samples could predict the strength of the classifier prediction at response time.
source: We found that the optimal evidence L, accumulated over all samples, could predict the strength of the classifier prediction at response time (mean β = 0.11, t(19) = 3.89, p < 0.001; Figure 3c).
evidence: This is a statistical finding from the exploratory analysis, with reference to Figure 3c.

claim: In the More condition, the evidence accumulated up to four samples prior to the response still predicted the strength of the classifier prediction.
source: But, in the More condition, the evidence accumulated up to four samples prior to the response still predicted the strength of the classifier prediction (t(19) = 3.81, p = 0.001).
evidence: This is a statistical finding from the exploratory analysis of the current study.

claim: There was a significant interaction between condition and samples accumulated in predicting the strength of the classifier prediction.
source: This difference between conditions over samples is evidenced by a significant interaction based on a repeated measures ANOVA (F(8,152) = 2.429, p = 0.05, after Bonferroni correction for three comparisons).
evidence: This is a statistical finding from the exploratory analysis of the current study.

claim: The optimal observer must encode the orientation of the stimulus, estimate the decision update based on the categories, and add this to the accumulated evidence for discriminating between the categories.
source: To perform this task the optimal observer must encode the orientation of the stimulus, estimate the decision update based on the categories, and add this to the accumulated evidence for discriminating between the categories (Wyart et al., 2012; Wyart et al., 2015).
evidence: This is a description of the optimal computation supported by citations to Wyart et al. (2012, 2015).

claim: The precision of the representations of stimulus orientation, momentary decision update, and accumulated evidence showed distinct time courses and relied on distinct patterns of EEG activity over scalp topography.
source: The precision of the representations of these variables showed distinct time courses and relied on distinct patterns of EEG activity over scalp topography (Figure 4b).
evidence: This is a finding from the EEG encoding analysis, with reference to Figure 4b.

claim: There was a transient representation of stimulus orientation localised over occipital electrodes.
source: There was a transient representation of stimulus orientation localised over occipital electrodes.
evidence: This is a finding from the EEG encoding analysis of the current study.

claim: The representation of the momentary decision update was maintained for a longer duration, initially supported by occipital electrodes, then increasingly localised over central-parietal electrodes.
source: The representation of the momentary decision update was maintained for a longer duration, initially supported by occipital electrodes, then increasingly localised over central-parietal electrodes.
evidence: This is a finding from the EEG encoding analysis of the current study.

claim: The representation of the accumulated evidence was sustained even longer and relied on both frontal and occipital electrodes.
source: The representation of the accumulated evidence was sustained even longer and relied on both frontal and occipital electrodes.
evidence: This is a finding from the EEG encoding analysis of the current study.

claim: The precision of the representation of stimulus orientation did not significantly vary based on whether behaviour matched the optimal response.
source: For each variable, we estimated the representation precision separately for epochs leading to behavioural responses that differed from the optimal response (based on L), and responses that matched those of the optimal observer (Replay task epochs only; Figure 4c; Appendix 3). For perceptual decisions, the optimal observer responds with the correct category. For confidence evaluations, the optimal observer gives high confidence on trials with greater than the median evidence (over all trials) for their perceptual response. The precision of the representation of stimulus orientation did not significantly vary based on whether behaviour matched the optimal response.
evidence: This is a statistical finding from the behavioral comparison analysis, with reference to Figure 4c.

claim: The representation precision of the momentary decision update showed a significant effect for the perceptual decision from 380 to 468 ms.
source: The representation precision of the momentary decision update showed a significant effect for the perceptual decision from 380 to 468 ms (Favg(1,19) = 7.97, pcluster = 0.008) and a significant interaction between perceptual and confidence responses from 396 to 468 ms (Favg(1,19) = 6.66, pcluster = 0.022) and from 716 to 856 ms (Favg(1,19) = 10.75, pcluster < 0.001).
evidence: This is a statistical finding from the behavioral comparison analysis of the current study.

claim: Representation precision of accumulated evidence was significantly reduced in epochs leading to non-optimal perceptual decisions from 108 ms post stimulus onset to the end of the epoch.
source: Representation precision was significantly reduced in epochs leading to non-optimal perceptual decisions from 108 ms post stimulus onset to the end of the epoch (Favg(1,19) = 13.65, pcluster <0.001).
evidence: This is a statistical finding from the behavioral comparison analysis of the current study.

claim: There was a significant interaction between perceptual and confidence responses in the representation precision of accumulated evidence from 696 to 836 ms.
source: In addition, there was a significant interaction with confidence from 696 to 836 ms (Favg(1,19) = 8.72, pcluster = 0.005).
evidence: This is a statistical finding from the behavioral comparison analysis of the current study.

claim: The precision of the early representation of accumulated evidence was significantly attenuated for the last four samples of the More condition compared to the last four samples of the Less condition.
source: Indeed, the precision of the early representation of accumulated evidence was significantly attenuated for the last four samples of the More condition (in which observers were likely to have already committed to a decision), compared to the last four samples of the Less condition (where observers were unlikely to have committed to a decision; from the start of the epoch to 424 ms, Figure 4d; tavg(19) = −5.19, pcluster<0.001).
evidence: This is a statistical finding from the condition comparison analysis, with reference to Figure 4d.

claim: Differences in representation precision between More and Less conditions were not present for the encoding of stimulus orientation nor the decision update.
source: These differences in representation precision were not present for the encoding of stimulus orientation, nor the decision update, suggesting that these processes may reflect input to perceptual evidence accumulation, but not the accumulation process itself.
evidence: This is a finding from the condition comparison analysis of the current study.

claim: Signals related to internal evidence for perceptual decisions were initially clustered over posterior electrodes, becoming dispersed over more anterior electrodes late in the epoch.
source: For perceptual decision-making, signals related to L* were initially clustered over posterior electrodes, becoming dispersed over more anterior electrodes late in the epoch (Figure 5a, top).
evidence: This is a finding from the Bayesian scan statistics analysis, with reference to Figure 5a.

claim: For confidence, two co-temporal clusters in posterior and anterior electrodes emerged from 668 ms to 824 ms from stimulus onset.
source: For confidence, we found two co-temporal clusters in posterior and anterior electrodes emerging from 668 ms to 824 ms from stimulus onset (Figure 5a, bottom).
evidence: This is a finding from the Bayesian scan statistics analysis, with reference to Figure 5a.

claim: An early posterior cluster of signals was strongly related to internal evidence for perceptual decisions but was not diagnostic of confidence evaluations.
source: In Figure 5a, we highlight an early posterior cluster of signals strongly related to L* for perceptual decisions, that was not diagnostic of confidence evaluations (in fact the evidence was in favour of the null hypothesis; summed log likelihood ratio = −1176).
evidence: This is a finding from the Bayesian scan statistics analysis, with reference to Figure 5a.

claim: Combining the perceptual and confidence clusters improves the representation precision.
source: That the information from these clusters is not redundant is evident from the fact that combining the clusters improves the representation precision (Figure 5b).
evidence: This is a finding from the cluster analysis, with reference to Figure 5b.

claim: The representation precision of the early posterior cluster was attenuated for the last four samples of the More condition.
source: Similar to the previous analysis (Figure 4d), the representation precision of the early posterior cluster was attenuated for the last four samples of the More condition.
evidence: This is a finding from the cluster analysis of the current study.

claim: The representation precision of the confidence cluster was maintained for the last four samples of the More condition.
source: But, the representation precision of the confidence cluster was maintained (a repeated measures ANOVA revealed a significant interaction between cluster and condition for decoding precision in the last four samples, F(1,19) = 32.00, p = 0.001, Bonferroni corrected for three comparisons).
evidence: This is a statistical finding from the cluster analysis of the current study.

claim: The estimate of single-sample inference error from the confidence cluster representation was significantly correlated with the single-sample inference error estimated from the computational model of confidence ratings.
source: This estimate of the single-sample inference error was significantly correlated with the single-sample inference error estimated from the computational model of confidence ratings (t(19) = 5.12, p < 0.001), and this correlation was significantly greater than the correlation with the error estimated from the model of perceptual decisions alone (t(19) = 2.62, p = 0.017; see Appendix 8).
evidence: This is a statistical finding from the model comparison analysis of the current study.

claim: Noise Max epochs showed a greater increase in current density power over time compared to Noise Min epochs.
source: As expected, Noise Max epochs showed a greater increase in current density power over time.
evidence: This is a finding from the source localization analysis of the current study.

claim: Significant differences between Noise Max and Noise Min epochs first emerged in the superior parietal cortex from 276 to 304 ms.
source: Significant differences first emerged in the superior parietal cortex (Figure 5d; 276 to 304 ms; tavg(19) = 2.37, pcluster = 0.016, re-emerging at 596 to 748 ms; tavg(19) = 2.53, pcluster = 0.016; and 912 ms; tavg(19) = 2.50, pcluster = 0.014), and then in the orbitofrontal cortex (OFC; 516 to 556 ms; tavg(19) = 2.30, pcluster = 0.022, re-emerging at 660 to 772 ms; tavg(19) = 2.79, pcluster = 0.032, and 824 to 1000 ms; tavg(19) = 2.60, pcluster = 0.022).
evidence: This is a statistical finding from the source localization analysis, with reference to Figure 5d.

claim: Significant differences between Noise Max and Noise Min epochs emerged in the orbitofrontal cortex from 516 to 556 ms.
source: Significant differences first emerged in the superior parietal cortex (Figure 5d; 276 to 304 ms; tavg(19) = 2.37, pcluster = 0.016, re-emerging at 596 to 748 ms; tavg(19) = 2.53, pcluster = 0.016; and 912 ms; tavg(19) = 2.50, pcluster = 0.014), and then in the orbitofrontal cortex (OFC; 516 to 556 ms; tavg(19) = 2.30, pcluster = 0.022, re-emerging at 660 to 772 ms; tavg(19) = 2.79, pcluster = 0.032, and 824 to 1000 ms; tavg(19) = 2.60, pcluster = 0.022).
evidence: This is a statistical finding from the source localization analysis, with reference to Figure 5d.

claim: No differences in the rostral middle frontal cortex nor lateral occipital cortex survived cluster correction.
source: No differences in the rostral middle frontal cortex nor lateral occipital cortex survived cluster correction.
evidence: This is a finding from the source localization analysis of the current study.

claim: Activity localised to the superior parietal cortex reflected stimulus driven computations.
source: Whilst the activity localised to the superior parietal cortex reflected stimulus driven computations (the consecutive peaks correspond temporally to the response to subsequent stimuli), the activity localised to the orbitofrontal cortex was more indicative of an accumulation process across samples (a smoother increase in signal over time).
evidence: This is an interpretation of the temporal dynamics observed in the source localization analysis.

claim: Activity localised to the orbitofrontal cortex was more indicative of an accumulation process across samples.
source: Whilst the activity localised to the superior parietal cortex reflected stimulus driven computations (the consecutive peaks correspond temporally to the response to subsequent stimuli), the activity localised to the orbitofrontal cortex was more indicative of an accumulation process across samples (a smoother increase in signal over time).
evidence: This is an interpretation of the temporal dynamics observed in the source localization analysis.

claim: The activity localised to the orbitofrontal cortex predicted observers' confidence ratings.
source: Indeed, the activity localised to the orbitofrontal cortex predicted observers' confidence ratings, based on the predictions of a generalised linear model with 90/10 cross validation: the standardised regression coefficients increased up to and continued after the perceptual decision response (Figure 5e, a significant cluster was located from −300 to 520 ms around the time of the response; tave(19) = 3.46, cluster-corrected p < 0.001).
evidence: This is a statistical finding from the exploratory GLM analysis, with reference to Figure 5e.

claim: Covert decisions could trigger the motor preparation for pressing the response key.
source: This suggests that covert decisions could trigger the motor preparation for pressing the response key.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the cross-classification analysis results.

claim: When observers committed to perceptual decisions prematurely, only the early part of the representation of accumulated evidence was attenuated.
source: When observers committed to perceptual decisions prematurely, only the early part of the representation of accumulated evidence was attenuated.
evidence: This is a finding from the EEG representation analysis of the current study.

claim: The representations of stimulus orientation and decision update did not substantially change after committing to a perceptual decision.
source: The representations of stimulus orientation and decision update (Wyart et al., 2012; Wyart et al., 2015; Weiss et al., 2021), which are necessary input for the perceptual decision, did not substantially change after committing to a perceptual decision.
evidence: This is a finding from the EEG representation analysis, with citations to related work.

claim: Initial perceptual processing likely remained important for the continued accumulation of evidence for evaluating confidence even after the completion of perceptual decision processes.
source: This initial perceptual processing stage likely remained important for the continued accumulation of evidence for evaluating confidence (even after the completion of perceptual decision processes), though it could also be that these processes are automatically triggered by stimulus onset irrespective of whether the evidence is being accumulated for decision-making.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the pattern of neural representations observed.

claim: The P300 and Central Parietal Positivity (CPP) have been found as neural correlates of confidence magnitude related to the accumulation of perceptual decision evidence.
source: Confidence should increase with increasing evidence for the perceptual decision. It is therefore unsurprising that the neural correlates of confidence magnitude have found similar EEG markers as those related to the accumulation of the underlying perceptual decision evidence: the P300 (Gherman and Philiastides, 2015; Desender et al., 2016; Desender et al., 2019; Zakrzewski et al., 2019; Rausch et al., 2020) and Central Parietal Positivity (CPP; Boldt et al., 2019; Herding et al., 2019, indeed we show a similar effect in Appendix 4).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to previous studies.

claim: Activity localised to the superior parietal and orbitofrontal cortices tracked the internal evidence for confidence throughout decision-making.
source: Activity localised to the superior parietal and orbitofrontal cortices was found to track this internal evidence for confidence throughout decision-making.
evidence: This is a finding from the source localization analysis of the current study.

claim: Confidence is based on information coded in parietal cortex where the underlying perceptual decision evidence is integrated.
source: The difference in superior parietal cortex could be linked with findings from electrophysiology that suggest that confidence is based on information coded in parietal cortex, where the underlying perceptual decision evidence is integrated (Kiani and Shadlen, 2009; Rutishauser et al., 2018; though at least a subset of these neurons reflect bounded accumulation, which is in contrast with the continued confidence accumulation described in this experiment; Kiani et al., 2008).
evidence: This is an interpretation connecting the current findings to previous electrophysiology studies, supported by citations.

claim: The orbitofrontal cortex has neural coding associated with stimulus value.
source: Early electrophysiological investigation into the function of the orbitofrontal cortex revealed neural coding associated with stimulus value (Thorpe et al., 1983), which has since been linked with a confidence-modulated signal of outcome-expectation (Kepecs et al., 2008; and in human fMRI; Rolls et al., 2010) and recently, shown to be domain-general (single OFC neurons were associated with confidence in both olfactory and auditory tasks; Masset et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Thorpe et al. (1983), Kepecs et al. (2008), Rolls et al. (2010), and Masset et al. (2020).

claim: The orbitofrontal cortex has been linked with a confidence-modulated signal of outcome-expectation.
source: Early electrophysiological investigation into the function of the orbitofrontal cortex revealed neural coding associated with stimulus value (Thorpe et al., 1983), which has since been linked with a confidence-modulated signal of outcome-expectation (Kepecs et al., 2008; and in human fMRI; Rolls et al., 2010) and recently, shown to be domain-general (single OFC neurons were associated with confidence in both olfactory and auditory tasks; Masset et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Kepecs et al. (2008) and Rolls et al. (2010).

claim: Single OFC neurons were associated with confidence in both olfactory and auditory tasks, showing domain-general confidence coding.
source: Early electrophysiological investigation into the function of the orbitofrontal cortex revealed neural coding associated with stimulus value (Thorpe et al., 1983), which has since been linked with a confidence-modulated signal of outcome-expectation (Kepecs et al., 2008; and in human fMRI; Rolls et al., 2010) and recently, shown to be domain-general (single OFC neurons were associated with confidence in both olfactory and auditory tasks; Masset et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Masset et al. (2020).

claim: Neural signatures of confidence evidence encoding were present throughout the process of making a perceptual decision.
source: These neural signatures of confidence evidence encoding were present throughout the process of making a perceptual decision.
evidence: This is a finding from the temporal analysis of neural representations in the current study.

claim: Confidence could be computed online, alongside perceptual evidence accumulation.
source: This is in line with more recent evidence suggesting that confidence could be computed online, alongside perceptual evidence accumulation (Zizlsperger et al., 2014; Gherman and Philiastides, 2015; Balsdon et al., 2020), as opposed to assessing the evidence in favour of the perceptual decision only after committing to that decision.
evidence: This is supported by citations to Zizlsperger et al. (2014), Gherman and Philiastides (2015), and Balsdon et al. (2020).

claim: The best description of confidence behaviour was an accumulation process that was partially dissociable from perceptual evidence accumulation.
source: Computational model comparison supported this interpretation, showing the best description of confidence behaviour was an accumulation process that was partially dissociable from perceptual evidence accumulation (Appendix 1; replicating our previous analysis, Balsdon et al., 2020).
evidence: This is a finding from the computational modeling analysis, replicating previous work.

claim: The partial dissociation between perceptual and confidence processes constrains confidence by perceptual suboptimalities while allowing additional processing to independently shape confidence.
source: This partial dissociation mediates the ongoing debate between single-channel (for example, Maniscalco and Lau, 2016) and dual-channel (for example, Charles et al., 2014) models, as it constrains confidence by perceptual suboptimalities, at the same time as allowing additional processing to independently shape confidence.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the computational modeling results in the context of theoretical debates, with citations.

claim: The combination of partial dissociation and online monitoring could allow for metacognitive control of perceptual evidence accumulation to flexibly balance perceptual accuracy against temporal efficiency.
source: The combination of this partial dissociation and online monitoring could allow for metacognitive control of perceptual evidence accumulation, to flexibly balance perceptual accuracy against temporal efficiency, by bounding perceptual evidence accumulation according to contemporaneous confidence.
evidence: This is a speculative inference about the functional implications of the findings.

claim: The perceptual representation neglected additional evidence following premature decision commitment whilst the confidence representation continued to track the updated evidence independently of decision commitment.
source: These neural representations were partially dissociable in that the perceptual representation neglected additional evidence following premature decision commitment whilst the confidence representation continued to track the updated evidence independently of decision commitment.
evidence: This is a summary finding from the neural representation analyses of the current study.

claim: The partial dissociation between perceptual and confidence neural representations validates the predictions of the computational model.
source: This partial dissociation validates the predictions of the computational model and provides a framework for the cognitive architecture underlying the distinction between perception and confidence.
evidence: This is an interpretation connecting the neural findings to the computational modeling results.

claim: The neural resources involved in the confidence representation can be recruited independently of perceptual processes, implying a specific neural circuit for the computation of confidence.
source: That the neural resources involved in the confidence representation can be recruited independently of perceptual processes implies a specific neural circuit for the computation of confidence, a necessary feature of a general metacognitive mechanism flexibly employed to monitor the validity of any cognitive process.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the dissociation observed in the neural representations.

claim: A specific neural circuit for confidence computation is a necessary feature of a general metacognitive mechanism flexibly employed to monitor the validity of any cognitive process.
source: That the neural resources involved in the confidence representation can be recruited independently of perceptual processes implies a specific neural circuit for the computation of confidence, a necessary feature of a general metacognitive mechanism flexibly employed to monitor the validity of any cognitive process.
evidence: This is a theoretical inference about the implications of the findings for understanding metacognition.

claim: Twenty participants were recruited from the local cognitive science mailing list and by word of mouth.
source: A total of 20 participants were recruited from the local cognitive science mailing list (RISC) and by word of mouth.
evidence: This is a description of the participant recruitment for the study.

claim: No participant met the pre-registered exclusion criteria of chance-level performance or excessive EEG noise.
source: No participant met the pre-registered (https://osf.io/346pe/) exclusion criteria of chance-level performance or excessive EEG noise.
evidence: This is a report of the data quality from the study.

claim: Stimuli were oriented Gabor patches displayed at 70% contrast, subtending four dva and with spatial frequency two cyc/deg.
source: Stimuli were oriented Gabor patches displayed at 70% contrast, subtending four dva and with spatial frequency two cyc/deg.
evidence: This is a description of the experimental stimuli.

claim: On each trial the orientations of the presented Gabors were drawn from one of two circular Gaussian (Von Mises) distributions centred on +/- 45° from vertical with concentration κ = 0.5.
source: On each trial the orientations of the presented Gabors were drawn from one of two circular Gaussian (Von Mises) distributions centred on +/- 45° from vertical (henceforth referred to as the 'orange' and 'blue' distributions, respectively), with concentration κ = 0.5 (shown in Figure 1d).
evidence: This is a description of the stimulus generation procedure, with reference to Figure 1d.

claim: In the Free task, observers were continually shown samples until they entered their response.
source: In the 'Free' task, observers were continually shown samples (up to 40) until they entered their response.
evidence: This is a description of the Free task procedure.

claim: In the Replay task, observers were shown a specific number of samples and could only enter their response after the sequence finished.
source: After completing the Free task, observers then completed the Replay task. In this task they were shown a specific number of samples and could only enter their response after the sequence finished, signalled by the fixation point turning red.
evidence: This is a description of the Replay task procedure.

claim: In the Less condition, observers were shown two fewer samples than the minimum they had chosen to respond to on that predefined sequence in the Free task.
source: There were three intermixed conditions: In the Less condition observers were shown two fewer samples than the minimum they had chosen to respond to on that predefined sequence in the Free task; In the Same condition observers were shown the median number of samples from that predefined sequence; in the More condition observers were shown four additional samples compared to the maximum number they chose to respond to on that sequence in the Free task.
evidence: This is a description of the Less condition in the Replay task.

claim: In the Same condition, observers were shown the median number of samples from that predefined sequence in the Free task.
source: There were three intermixed conditions: In the Less condition observers were shown two fewer samples than the minimum they had chosen to respond to on that predefined sequence in the Free task; In the Same condition observers were shown the median number of samples from that predefined sequence; in the More condition observers were shown four additional samples compared to the maximum number they chose to respond to on that sequence in the Free task.
evidence: This is a description of the Same condition in the Replay task.

claim: In the More condition, observers were shown four additional samples compared to the maximum number they chose to respond to on that sequence in the Free task.
source: There were three intermixed conditions: In the Less condition observers were shown two fewer samples than the minimum they had chosen to respond to on that predefined sequence in the Free task; In the Same condition observers were shown the median number of samples from that predefined sequence; in the More condition observers were shown four additional samples compared to the maximum number they chose to respond to on that sequence in the Free task.
evidence: This is a description of the More condition in the Replay task.
